title: Four Weddings in Mithila
captions: The next morning, King Janaka sent swift messengers to the city of Sankashya to bring his younger brother Kushadhvaja. Kushadhvaja came at once and bowed to his elder brother with love.
In the royal hall, Vasishtha proudly told the long line of Rama's ancestors, from Lord Brahma down to King Dasharatha. Then Janaka told the story of his own family, the kings of Mithila.
“I give my daughter Sita to Rama, and my daughter Urmila to Lakshmana,” said Janaka joyfully. “Let the weddings take place in three days, on a blessed day.”
Then Vishvamitra and Vasishtha said, “Kushadhvaja has two daughters too, Mandavi and Shrutakirti. Let them marry Bharata and Shatrughna.” Janaka and Kushadhvaja happily agreed.
Before the weddings, King Dasharatha gave a hundred thousand cows for each of his four sons to holy brahmanas. The cows had horns covered in gold, and he prayed for blessings on his boys.
On the wedding day, Vasishtha lit the sacred fire. Janaka brought Sita to Rama and said, “This is my daughter Sita. She will walk with you on the path of dharma. Take her hand in yours.”
Lakshmana, Bharata and Shatrughna took the hands of Urmila, Mandavi and Shrutakirti. The four couples walked around the sacred fire, and flowers rained down from the sky as the devas played music.
lesson: When great joy came to King Janaka, he did not keep it to himself. He sent for his younger brother Kushadhvaja, and the wise sages made sure Kushadhvaja's daughters were part of the celebration too, so all four brothers were married on the same happy day. In our tradition, Kutumba means family, and our elders teach that joy grows bigger when we share it with the people we love. That day in Mithila, two royal families became one big family.
card_lesson: King Janaka shared his joy with his brother, and all four princes were married on the same day. Kutumba means loving and including our family.
question: What is something your family loves to do together, and who would you invite to share it?
